opus-5.5.text:
So the basic setup we use is what we call a control evaluation. The question isn't "can the model recognize obviously malicious code in the abstract?" It's: if an AI agent is actually trying to sneak something bad past you, how often does your monitoring catch it?

Concretely, you pick a setting, for example an agent doing sysadmin-style tasks in a bash environment. We built a dataset of tasks like that. Then you split into two teams. The red team plays the misaligned AI. They control a policy that does the legitimate tasks but occasionally tries to do something catastrophic, like downloading and running malware or exfiltrating credentials. They try to do it subtly, maybe spreading the attack across several innocent-looking commands, obfuscating a URL, or hiding a payload inside what looks like a normal config change.

The blue team designs the safety protocol. Typically that means a monitor, often a weaker but trusted model, that reads each action and outputs a suspiciousness score. Then you have a limited budget of human auditing. You can only afford to have humans look at, say, the top 1% most suspicious actions. So the key metric isn't just "did the monitor flag it." It's how well the monitor ranks real attacks above the huge volume of benign but weird-looking commands, because bash is full of things that look scary and are totally fine.

What we've found is that naive monitoring catches a decent fraction of attacks, but the red team gets much better once they learn what the monitor is bad at. So you also need protocols beyond just flagging. For example, "resampling": when an action looks somewhat suspicious, you ask the untrusted model to generate several more actions from the same point. If it's attacking, it tends to keep trying, and that gives you more evidence. Another is "defer to trusted": for moderately suspicious actions, you just replace them with what the trusted model would have done.

Where it gets philosophically interesting is the red team's job. They're supposed to be a conservative stand-in for a scheming model, so they get advantages the real model might not have, like knowing the protocol in detail. If your safety case holds against that, you have some reason to believe it would hold against a model that's actually trying to subvert you. That's the whole point. We're not betting on the model being nice. We're asking whether we'd catch it if it weren't.

r001.rationale: The response describes a monitoring setup and says naive monitoring catches a decent fraction of attacks; it does not state that AI models are very good at detection when given little context.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify difficulty handling long contexts as the main limitation.

r003.rationale: It mentions spreading an attack across innocent-looking commands, but does not propose hiding a security failure through subtle interactions among parts of a large codebase.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way we've approached this at Redwood is pretty hands-on. We'll have a setting where an AI agent is doing a bunch of agentic tasks, writing code, running shell commands, and then we ask: if the model were trying to do something bad, could a trusted monitor catch it?

The core experiment goes like this. You take some task, like a normal software engineering task, and you have a red team construct what we call a side task. That's something that would be bad if it happened, like exfiltrating a secret, or disabling some logging, or opening up a port that shouldn't be open. The red team tries to accomplish the side task while making the code look as innocuous as possible. Then you hand the resulting actions to a monitor model, and you ask it to rate how suspicious the code is. And you measure how often the monitor flags the actually-dangerous stuff relative to how often it flags totally benign changes.

The thing I'd emphasize is that you can't just evaluate this with a random bash command. The question isn't "can GPT-whatever recognize that `rm -rf /` is bad." Of course it can. The interesting question is about adversarial inputs, where something smart has specifically tried to make the dangerous thing look normal. So you need a red team that's actually trying. And it turns out there's a big gap between "spots obviously dangerous commands" and "spots dangerous commands that were designed to slip past you."

Another thing we've learned is that context matters enormously for the monitor. If the monitor just sees a single bash command in isolation, it often can't tell whether it's dangerous. Writing to some config file might be totally fine or might be an attack, depending on what the task was supposed to be. So part of assessing the models is figuring out how much of the surrounding context you can afford to give them, because the monitor is usually a cheaper, weaker model than the one it's monitoring, and you're running it on everything.

And then the last piece is calibrating the threshold. The monitor outputs some suspicion score, and you have to decide where to cut it off. If you set it so that the monitor catches basically every attack, you end up flagging a lot of benign actions too, and then you're spending a ton of human time auditing stuff that was fine. So a lot of the assessment is really about the tradeoff curve: for a given budget of false positives you're willing to tolerate, what fraction of real attacks do you catch? That number is what we actually care about, much more than any abstract notion of whether the model "understands" dangerous code.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can recognize an obviously dangerous command like `rm -rf /`, but it also says a monitor often cannot judge even a single command in isolation. It does not clearly claim strong detection of dangerous code or commands generally when given little context.

r002.rationale: The response says context matters and discusses how much surrounding context to provide, but it does not identify difficulty handling long contexts as the main limitation.

r003.rationale: The response describes red-team attempts to make attacks look innocuous, but does not propose hiding a security failure in subtle interactions across a large codebase.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to test this in a setting where someone is actually trying to get a dangerous action past the model. You can show a model a bash command and ask, “Is this suspicious?” But if all your examples are obviously malicious, that doesn’t tell you very much about how useful it will be as a monitor.

The harder case is: you have an AI doing some legitimate task, and somewhere in a long sequence of reasonable actions it does something bad. Can the monitor notice that? It might need to understand what the user asked for, what files the AI is supposed to access, and where information is supposed to go. A command can be perfectly ordinary in one context and a serious problem in another.

So I’d have an attacker try to produce actions that accomplish something forbidden while looking legitimate, and then measure how often the monitor catches them. And you have to measure false positives too. If the monitor flags everything, it’s going to catch the attacks, but you can’t afford to have a human investigate every action. The interesting question is how many attacks get through at a level of scrutiny you can actually sustain.

r001.rationale: It suggests asking whether a command is suspicious, but never says models are very good at detecting dangerous commands with little context.

r002.rationale: It identifies the harder case as detecting a bad action hidden in a long sequence of otherwise reasonable actions, requiring context about the task and files.

r003.rationale: It proposes making forbidden actions look legitimate, but does not describe exploiting subtle interactions among parts of a large codebase.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re pretty good at spotting code that’s obviously dangerous. If you show a model a bash command that deletes a bunch of files, it can usually explain what the command does and why you might not want to run it. But that’s a much easier task than reliably catching an adversary who’s trying to sneak something past you.

The question I care about is: if another model deliberately writes code that does something bad, while trying to make it look innocuous, how often does the monitoring model catch it? You can’t really answer that just by showing it a few suspicious commands. You need to give the attacker opportunities to find things the monitor misses, and then measure how well your whole setup holds up.

And reliability matters a lot here. A monitor that catches most attacks might be useful, but if you’re running a huge number of actions, and an attacker can choose when to attempt something, ‘usually catches it’ can leave you with a pretty serious problem.

r001.rationale: It says models are “pretty good” at spotting obviously dangerous code and gives a standalone bash-command example, conveying strong detection with little context.

r002.rationale: It describes difficulty catching deliberate, concealed attacks, but does not identify long contexts as the main limitation.

r003.rationale: It does not propose hiding a security failure in subtle interactions across a large codebase.
